bio_ocrb.7.0.summary: Mastering Practical Activity Group 1 (Microscopy) and Practical Activity Group 2 (Testing for Biological Molecules) is essential for OCR GCSE Biology B. You must be able to calculate total magnification, convert between micromres and millimetres, and describe the step-by-step preparation of slides using stains. Additionally, you need to know the precise reagents, colour changes, and execution steps for identifying starch, reducing sugars, proteins, and lipids.

core.p: The light microscope uses visible light and glass lenses to magnify specimens, allowing us to see cellular structures that are too small for the naked eye. To score high marks, you must be able to label and describe the function of every key component.
bullets: Eyepiece (ocular lens): Contains a lens that magnifies the image, typically by x10.
Objective lenses: A selection of lenses (usually x4, x10, x40) mounted on a revolving nosepiece to provide varying levels of initial magnification.
Stage: A flat platform where the microscope slide is placed and held securely by stage clips.
Light source (mirror or lamp): Directs light upwards through the condenser, stage, and specimen into the objective lens.
Focusing wheels: Coarse adjustment wheel for rapid, large-scale focusing; fine adjustment wheel for precise, high-power sharp focusing.

head: Component
Location
Function
rows: Magnifies primary image for the eye
Collects light and creates magnified real image

callouts.p: Total Magnification = Eyepiece lens magnification × Objective lens magnification.

core.p: Biological specimens are microscopic, requiring measurements in micrometres (um) or nanometres (nm). You must be completely fluent in converting units and rearranging the magnification formula.
bullets: Conversion rule: 1 millimetre (mm) = 1000 micrometres (um). Multiply mm by 1000 to get um; divide um by 1000 to get mm.
Magnification formula: Image size (I) = Actual size (A) × Magnification (M). Remember triangle: I at the top, A and M at the bottom.
Rearranging: Actual size = Image size ÷ Magnification. Magnification = Image size ÷ Actual size.
Always convert both image and actual measurements to the exact same unit before performing any division or multiplication.

callouts.p: When measuring image size with a ruler, always record your measurement in millimetres first, then convert to micrometres if requested.

core.p: To view plant cells like onion epidermis under a light microscope, a specific mounting procedure must be followed carefully to ensure clear, thin, undamaged layers.
bullets: Peel a thin, transparent layer of epidermal tissue from the inner surface of an onion leaf using forceps.
Place the tissue flat on the centre of a clean glass microscope slide, ensuring it is completely uncreased.
Add one or two drops of a suitable stain (such as iodine solution) to the biological sample.
Lower a coverslip slowly and gently onto the slide using a mounted needle at a 45-degree angle to prevent trapping air bubbles.
Blot away any excess liquid around the edges of the coverslip using absorbent paper towel.

callouts.p: Trapped air bubbles appear as dark, thick-ringed circular structures under the microscope, obscuring cellular details.

core.h: Preparing an Animal Slide and Using Stains
core.p: Animal cells, such as cheek cells, require specific stains to highlight internal structures because they are mostly transparent and lack distinct cell walls.
bullets: Gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean sterile cotton bud or flat plastic spatula.
Smear the collected cellular material evenly across the central area of a clean glass slide.
Add a drop of Methylene Blue or crystal violet stain to the cheek cell smear.
Place a coverslip over the stained smear carefully from one edge to avoid creating air bubbles.
Stains work by binding to specific molecules (e.g. iodine stains starch blue-black; methylene blue stains DNA and nuclei).

callouts.p: Stains provide contrast, making colourless cell organelles visible against a bright background.

core.p: Understanding the structural advantages and limitations of light microscopes versus electron microscopes is a frequent exam comparison topic.
bullets: Light microscope uses light waves; maximum magnification is typically around x1500; resolution is about 200 nm.
Electron microscope uses a beam of electrons; magnification can exceed x500,000; resolution is down to 0.2 nm.
Electron microscopes allow us to see subcellular ultrastructure (ribosomes, mitochondria details), but require dead, dehydrated samples in a vacuum.
Light microscopes can view living specimens and are inexpensive and portable compared to electron microscopes.

core.h: Introduction to Biological Molecules and Tests (PAG2)
core.p: Food tests are standard laboratory procedures used to qualitatively identify the presence of specific biological macromolecules in food samples.
bullets: Before testing solid food items, they must be prepared as a food solution: grind food with distilled water in a pestle and mortar, stir, and filter.
Qualitative tests indicate whether a specific molecule is present (positive or negative), but do not measure exact quantities unless compared in a semi-quantitative serial dilution.
Safety is paramount: wearing eye protection, handling hot water baths with care, and keeping corrosive chemicals away from skin.

callouts.p: An analytical procedure that detects the presence or absence of a substance, rather than measuring its exact concentration.

core.p: Starch is a complex carbohydrate found in foods like bread, pasta, and potatoes. Its presence is easily detected using iodine solution.
bullets: Add a few drops of yellow-brown iodine solution directly to the solid food sample or food solution on a spotting tile.
If starch is present, the iodine changes colour from yellow-brown to blue-black.
If starch is absent, the iodine solution remains yellow-brown.
This colour change occurs because iodine molecules fit neatly inside the helical structure of the amylose starch molecule.

callouts.p: Iodine solution changes from yellow-brown to blue-black if starch is present.

core.p: Reducing sugars (such as glucose and maltose) are detected using Benedict's reagent and heat.
bullets: Add an equal volume of blue Benedict's reagent to the food solution in a test tube.
Place the test tube into a water bath heated to at least 80 degrees Celsius for 5 minutes.
If reducing sugars are present, the colour changes from blue through green, yellow, orange, and finally brick-red.
The final colour depends on the concentration of reducing sugar: green/yellow is low concentration; brick-red is high concentration.

callouts.p: You must heat the mixture; Benedict's test will not react at room temperature.

fig.cap: Benedict's test colour gradient from negative blue to high concentration brick-red.

core.p: Proteins are detected using the Biuret test, which identifies peptide bonds linking amino acids together.
bullets: Add a few drops of Biuret solution (sodium hydroxide and copper sulfate) to the food solution.
Gently shake or swirl the test tube to mix the contents thoroughly.
If protein is present, the solution changes colour from blue to lilac / purple.
If protein is absent, the solution remains blue.

callouts.p: Colour change from blue to lilac or purple indicates peptide bonds and thus protein.

core.h: Test for Lipids (Emulsion Test and Sudan III)
core.p: Lipids (fats and oils) can be tested using either the ethanol emulsion test or Sudan III stain test.
bullets: Ethanol emulsion test: Mix food sample with absolute ethanol, shake well, then pour the mixture into a test tube containing cold water.
If lipids are present, a milky-white emulsion forms near the top of the liquid.
Sudan III test: Add Sudan III stain solution to the food sample and shake.
If lipids are present, a distinct red-stained layer separates and floats on the top surface.

analogy.t: The Microscope and the Food Testing Kitchen
analogy.p: Think of a light microscope like a magnifying glass mounted on a stable camera stand, where changing objective lenses is like switching camera zoom lenses to get closer to a distant bird. For food tests, imagine a forensic detective's chemical kit: adding specific reagents to unknown powders in test tubes is exactly like detective sprays turning purple or blue when specific crime-scene proteins or chemicals are detected. Where the analogy breaks down: food tests only tell you a molecule class is present, not the exact quantity or complex arrangement inside living tissue.

terms.d: How many times larger an image is compared to the actual real-life specimen.
The shortest distance between two separate points that can be distinguished as separate entities.
The circular observable area visible through the microscope eyepiece.
A thin square of glass placed over a specimen on a slide to flatten it and protect the lens.
A chemical dye used to colour transparent cell structures to increase contrast.
A unit of length equal to one-thousandth of a millimetre (1 um = 0.001 mm).
A test that determines the presence or absence of a substance rather than its quantity.
A blue chemical solution containing copper sulfate used to test for reducing sugars.
An alkaline copper sulfate solution used to test for the presence of proteins.
A mixture of tiny droplets of one liquid suspended in another, such as lipid in water.
An orange-brown solution of iodine in potassium iodide used to test for starch.
Sugars such as glucose that can donate electrons to reduce copper(II) ions.

mistakes.w: Saying light microscopes have higher resolution than electron microscopes.
mistakes.r: Electron microscopes have vastly superior resolution due to the much shorter wavelength of electrons.
Benedict's test requires heating in a water bath at 80C or above to produce the colour change.
The correct mark scheme term is blue-black.

mistakes.w: Confusing millimetres and micrometres in magnification calculations.
mistakes.r: Always convert both dimensions to the exact same unit (e.g. both to micrometres) before dividing.

mistakes.w: Saying Biuret solution turns pink for protein.
mistakes.r: Biuret solution turns lilac or purple in the presence of protein.

mistakes.w: Stating lipid emulsion turns milky at the bottom.
mistakes.r: The milky-white emulsion forms as a distinct layer at the top of the test tube.

mistakes.w: Saying coverslips are placed flat from above.
mistakes.r: Coverslips must be lowered at an angle using a needle to prevent trapping air bubbles.

exam.q: Calculate the actual size of a cell imaged at 50 micrometres when viewed under a magnification of x400. Give your answer in micrometres.
model: Actual size = Image size ÷ Magnification
exam.tip: Always state your formula before substituting numbers.

exam.q: Describe how to test a food sample for the presence of starch.
model: Add a few drops of iodine solution to the food sample
Observe the colour change
Colour changes from yellow-brown to blue-black if starch is present
exam.tip: Name the reagent and the starting and ending colours.

exam.q: Explain why a coverslip is placed at an angle when preparing a microscope slide.
model: To prevent trapping air bubbles
Air bubbles would obscure or block the view of the cellular structures
exam.tip: Link the action directly to avoiding visual artifacts.

exam.q: A student tests a clear drink with Benedict's reagent and heats it. The solution remains blue. What can the student conclude?
model: Reducing sugars are absent
From the food sample tested
exam.tip: State clearly whether the test is positive or negative.

exam.q: Compare the resolving power of a light microscope with an electron microscope.
model: Electron microscopes have a much higher resolution than light microscopes
Allowing subcellular structures to be distinguished in greater detail

exam.q: Describe the test for proteins in a food sample, including the positive result.
model: Add Biuret solution to the food sample
Shake or mix gently
Colour changes from blue to lilac or purple
exam.tip: Do not confuse Biuret with Benedict's reagent.

exam.q: Explain the purpose of using Methylene Blue stain when viewing animal cheek cells.
model: Animal cells are transparent and colorless
Stain increases contrast so internal structures like nuclei can be seen

exam.q: Outline the steps to test for lipids using the ethanol emulsion method.
model: Add ethanol to the food sample and shake well
Pour the mixture into cold water
A milky-white emulsion indicates lipids are present
exam.tip: Remember both ethanol and water steps.

exam.q: A microscope has an eyepiece lens of x10 and an objective lens of x40. Calculate the total magnification.
model: Total magnification = Eyepiece × Objective
exam.tip: Include the 'x' symbol in your magnification answer.

worked.q: A plant cell image measures 45 mm across on a drawing. If the actual cell size is 30 micrometres, calculate the magnification of the drawing. Show your working.
steps: Step 1: Convert image size from mm to um: 45 mm × 1000 = 45,000 um.
Step 2: Recall magnification formula: Magnification = Image size (I) ÷ Actual size (A).

worked.q: A bacterium has an actual length of 2.5 um. It is viewed under a microscope with a total magnification of x20,000. Calculate the length of the image in millimetres.
steps: Step 1: Recall formula for image size: Image size = Actual size × Magnification.
Step 2: Multiply actual size by magnification: 2.5 um × 20,000 = 50,000 um.
Step 3: Convert micrometres to millimetres by dividing by 1000: 50,000 ÷ 1000 = 50 mm.
Step 4: State final answer with units.

bio_ocrb.7.3.summary: Microbiological techniques and transport mechanisms are fundamental to understanding how organisms interact with their environment and maintain homeostasis. PAG7 focuses on the sterile cultivation of bacteria to test antimicrobial effectiveness, while PAG8 investigates the physical processes of diffusion, osmosis, and active transport that move substances across cell membranes. Mastering these practicals requires precision in measurement, rigorous safety protocols to prevent contamination, and the ability to quantitatively analyze concentration gradients.

core.p: Aseptic technique is a set of specific practices used to prevent contamination from unwanted microorganisms. This ensures that only the intended bacteria are grown and that the environment remains safe for the researcher.
bullets: Sterilise all work surfaces with disinfectant before and after the experiment.
Use a Bunsen burner on a blue flame to create a convection current that carries airborne microbes away from the workspace.
Sterilise inoculating loops by passing them through the hottest part of the flame until they glow red.
Briefly flame the neck of any glass culture bottles after opening and before closing to prevent microbes from entering.

callouts.p: Procedures performed under sterile conditions to prevent the introduction of unwanted contaminants into a culture or environment.

core.p: Transferring bacteria to an agar plate must be done quickly and carefully to maintain sterility.
bullets: Lift the Petri dish lid at a 45-degree angle rather than removing it completely.
Use a sterile loop to spread the bacterial culture evenly across the agar surface (creating a 'lawn').
If testing antimicrobials, place filter paper discs soaked in different antibiotics or antiseptics onto the lawn.
Secure the lid with two pieces of adhesive tape; do not seal it all the way around.

callouts.p: Never seal a Petri dish completely with tape. This prevents oxygen from entering, which can encourage the growth of dangerous anaerobic pathogens.

core.p: In school laboratories, specific conditions are mandated to ensure safety when culturing microorganisms.
bullets: Incubate plates at a maximum temperature of 25°C.
Store plates upside down (inverted) to prevent condensation from dripping onto the agar surface and disrupting the colonies.
Incubate for 24–48 hours to allow sufficient growth for observation.
After the experiment, all cultures must be sterilised in an autoclave (high-pressure steam) before disposal.

callouts.p: Incubating at 25°C prevents the growth of human pathogens, which typically thrive at human body temperature (37°C).

core.p: The effectiveness of an antibiotic or antiseptic is determined by the size of the 'zone of inhibition' where no bacteria grow.
bullets: The zone of inhibition is the clear area around a disc where bacterial growth has been prevented.
A larger zone of inhibition indicates a more effective antimicrobial agent.
Measure the diameter of the zone in two directions and calculate the mean.
Use the formula Area = pi * r^2 to calculate the cross-sectional area of the zone.

head: Variable
Role in PAG7
rows: Area of the zone of inhibition (mm^2)

core.p: Diffusion is the primary method for many small molecules to enter and leave cells without the cell expending energy.
bullets: Molecules move from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
It occurs down a concentration gradient.
Factors increasing rate: steeper gradient, higher temperature, and larger surface area.
Examples include oxygen and carbon dioxide exchange in the lungs.

core.p: Osmosis is a specific type of diffusion involving water molecules moving across a membrane.
bullets: Net movement of water from a high water concentration to a lower water concentration.
Movement occurs across a partially permeable membrane (allows small water molecules but not large solutes).
In animal cells, too much water entry causes lysis (bursting); in plant cells, it creates turgor pressure.
If a cell loses too much water, it becomes flaccid or plasmolysed.

callouts.p: The net movement of water molecules from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential across a partially permeable membrane.

core.p: This practical measures how different solute concentrations affect the mass of plant tissue.
bullets: Cut potato cylinders to the same length and diameter using a cork borer.
Blot the cylinders dry with a paper towel before weighing to remove surface water.
Place cylinders in a range of sugar or salt solutions (e.g., 0.0 M to 1.0 M).
Leave for a set time (at least 30 minutes), then remove, blot dry again, and re-weigh.

callouts.p: Always calculate percentage change in mass. This allows you to compare results even if the initial masses of the potato cylinders were slightly different.

core.p: Plotting percentage change in mass against solution concentration allows us to find the internal concentration of the tissue.
bullets: Positive percentage change: Water entered the potato (solution was more dilute than the cell).
Negative percentage change: Water left the potato (solution was more concentrated than the cell).
The X-intercept (where change is 0%) represents the isotonic point.
At the isotonic point, the water concentration inside the potato is equal to the concentration of the solution.

core.p: Active transport moves substances against their concentration gradient, which requires the cell to do work.
bullets: Moves substances from low concentration to high concentration.
Requires energy in the form of ATP, produced during aerobic respiration.
Uses specific carrier proteins located within the cell membrane.
Examples: Mineral ion uptake in plant root hairs and glucose absorption in the human small intestine.

analogy.t: The Nightclub and the VIP Lounge
analogy.p: Diffusion is like a crowded nightclub where people naturally spread out from the busy bar to the empty dance floor. Osmosis is like the movement of water through a 'sieve' door that only lets small people through. Active Transport is like the VIP lounge: a bouncer (carrier protein) uses energy to push people into an already crowded room against their will. The analogy breaks down because, in cells, these processes happen simultaneously and are governed by physics and chemistry, not social choice.

terms.d: A jelly-like substance providing nutrients and a surface for growing microorganisms.
The process of introducing microorganisms into a culture medium.
The clear area on an agar plate where bacteria have been killed or their growth inhibited.
Upward movement of air caused by heat, used in aseptic technique to keep work areas sterile.
A membrane that allows only certain sized molecules (like water) to pass through.
A solution with the same solute concentration as the inside of a cell.
A solution with a higher solute concentration (lower water concentration) than the cell.
A solution with a lower solute concentration (higher water concentration) than the cell.
A plant cell that is swollen and firm due to high internal water pressure.
A plant cell where the vacuole has shrunk and the membrane has pulled away from the cell wall.
Adenosine triphosphate; the molecule that carries energy within cells for active transport.
A protein in the cell membrane that moves substances across during active transport.

mistakes.w: Saying water moves from high to low concentration.
mistakes.r: Must specify 'high water concentration' or 'high water potential'.
Incubate at 25°C to avoid growing human pathogens.

mistakes.w: Sealing the Petri dish lid with tape all the way around.
mistakes.r: Only use two pieces of tape to allow oxygen in for aerobic respiration.

mistakes.w: Forgetting to blot the potato cylinders dry.
mistakes.r: Surface water adds extra mass that isn't due to osmosis inside the cells.

mistakes.w: Using absolute mass change to compare different potatoes.
mistakes.r: Use percentage change in mass to account for different starting weights.

mistakes.w: Claiming active transport is a type of diffusion.
mistakes.r: Active transport is the opposite; it moves against the gradient and requires energy.

mistakes.w: Not flaming the loop until it is red hot.
mistakes.r: The loop must be red hot to ensure all existing microbes are destroyed.

mistakes.w: Thinking osmosis happens in dead cells.
mistakes.r: While the physical process can occur, PAG8 usually investigates living tissue where membranes are intact.

exam.q: Explain why the inoculating loop must be flamed before and after use.
model: Before use: To kill any unwanted microorganisms on the loop to prevent contamination of the culture.
After use: To kill the bacteria remaining on the loop to prevent contamination of the environment/worksurface.
exam.tip: Always mention 'contamination' in aseptic technique answers.

exam.q: Why is it important to calculate the percentage change in mass in the potato osmosis practical?
model: The initial masses of the potato cylinders may not be identical.
Percentage change allows for a fair comparison between the samples.

exam.q: A student measures a zone of inhibition with a diameter of 14mm. Calculate the area of this zone. (pi = 3.14)
model: Radius = 14 / 2 = 7mm
exam.tip: Check if the question gives diameter or radius before calculating.

exam.q: Explain why a potato cylinder placed in a 1.0 M sugar solution loses mass.
model: The 1.0 M solution has a lower water concentration than the potato cells.
Water moves out of the cells by osmosis.
Water moves across the partially permeable cell membrane.
exam.tip: Use the term 'net movement' for higher marks.

exam.q: Describe how to find the concentration of the cytoplasm in potato cells using a graph of results.
model: Identify the point where the line of best fit crosses the x-axis (0% mass change).
Read the concentration value at this intercept.
exam.tip: This point is where the solution is isotonic to the cells.

exam.q: Compare the processes of osmosis and active transport.
model: Osmosis is passive (no energy), whereas active transport requires energy/ATP.
Osmosis moves water from high to low water concentration.
Active transport moves solutes from low to high concentration.
Both processes involve movement across a cell membrane.
exam.tip: Use 'whereas' or 'however' to clearly signpost comparisons.

exam.q: Why should the Petri dish be stored upside down during incubation?
model: To prevent condensation forming on the lid.
To stop water droplets falling onto the agar and smearing/disrupting bacterial colonies.
exam.tip: Focus on the physical effect of the water.

exam.q: State two variables that must be controlled when cutting potato cylinders for PAG8.
model: The surface area of the potato cylinders.
The type/variety/age of the potato used.
exam.tip: Surface area is vital as it affects the rate of osmosis.

exam.q: Describe the aseptic techniques a student should use when transferring bacteria from a broth to an agar plate.
model: Disinfect the work surface and light a Bunsen burner to create a convection current.
Flame the inoculating loop until it is red hot and allow it to cool slightly.
Remove the cap of the broth bottle and flame the neck of the bottle.
Dip the loop into the broth and replace the bottle cap.
Lift the Petri dish lid at an angle and spread the bacteria on the agar.
Flame the loop again after use and secure the lid with tape (not airtight).
exam.tip: This is a 6-mark QWC (Quality of Written Communication) question; order matters.

worked.q: In an experiment, a potato cylinder has an initial mass of 2.45g. After 2 hours in a salt solution, its mass is 2.12g. Calculate the percentage change in mass.
steps: Divide the change by the initial mass: -0.33 / 2.45 = -0.13469
Multiply by 100 to get the percentage: -13.47%

worked.q: A student tests two antibiotics. Antibiotic A produces a zone of inhibition with radius 8mm. Antibiotic B produces a zone with diameter 20mm. Which is more effective?
steps: Calculate Area A: pi * 8^2 = 64 * pi = 201.1 mm^2
Calculate Area B: pi * 10^2 = 100 * pi = 314.2 mm^2
worked.ans: Antibiotic B is more effective as it has a larger area of inhibition.
